nameStory: The narrow-winged tree cricket gets its name from its slender wing covers that are noticeably thinner than those of its broad-winged cousins. It's also sometimes called the snowy tree cricket because of its pale, almost translucent appearance that can look ghostly white in moonlight.
description: This delicate tree cricket is a pale, almost transparent insect about half an inch long with long, thread-like antennae. Males have narrow, oval wing covers they rub together to create their musical chirping, while females have a long, needle-like egg-laying tube called an ovipositor. Their bodies are typically cream-colored to pale green, helping them blend in perfectly with leaves and stems. Despite being called 'tree' crickets, they're equally at home in shrubs and tall grasses.

idTips.label: Wing Shape
idTips.description: Males have distinctly narrow, elongated wing covers that don't overlap much when folded - they look almost rectangular compared to the broader, more oval wings of related species

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Overall pale cream to light green coloration with a translucent quality - hold one gently and you can almost see through parts of its body

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Thread-like antennae that are often longer than the entire body, constantly moving and feeling around - they feel delicate as silk if they brush against your hand

idTips.label: Female Ovipositor
idTips.description: Females have a prominent, straight, needle-like egg-laying tube extending from the rear that's about as long as the body

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Slender build about half an inch long with long, thin legs that feel surprisingly delicate when handled - much more fragile-seeming than ground crickets

habitat: Found in shrubs, small trees, and tall herbaceous plants throughout New England's forests, forest edges, and overgrown fields. They particularly favor areas with mixed deciduous growth and are often found on elderberry, dogwood, and various flowering shrubs. Look for them anywhere from ground level to about 10 feet up, especially in areas that stay somewhat moist.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active. Previous year's eggs are developing in plant stems and bark crevices.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults emerge and begin their nightly concerts. Males sing most actively on warm, humid evenings from July through August.
seasonality.fall: Singing continues into September and early October, with mating and egg-laying occurring. Adults die off with the first hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: Only eggs survive the winter, tucked safely inside plant stems where they'll wait until the following summer to hatch.

funFact: Male narrow-winged tree crickets are living thermometers - you can actually calculate the temperature by counting their chirps! Count the number of chirps in 13 seconds and add 40 to get the temperature in Fahrenheit, and they're accurate to within a few degrees.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the snowy tree cricket and broad-winged tree cricket, but the narrow-winged has distinctly slimmer, more rectangular wing covers on males. Remember: narrow wings = narrow-winged cricket. The broad-winged species has obviously wider, more oval wings that overlap more when folded.
contextualKnowledge: There's some naming confusion since this species is sometimes also called the 'snowy tree cricket,' the same common name used for a close relative (Oecanthus fultoni). When reading about tree crickets, pay attention to the scientific names to avoid mix-ups, as common names can vary by region and source.
compareHints: Among New England's tree crickets, this species stands out for its narrow wing shape compared to the broad-winged tree cricket's obviously wider wings. It lacks the distinctive black markings found on black-horned and four-spotted tree crickets, and it's typically found in broader habitats than the pine tree cricket, which sticks mainly to coniferous trees.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's tree crickets, Pine Tree Cricket is unique in its exclusive preference for pine trees - Snowy Tree Crickets prefer deciduous trees and shrubs, while Broad-winged Tree Crickets favor fruit trees and berry bushes.
Among New England's tree crickets, the Black-horned is the easiest to identify thanks to its dark antennae.

Among New England's tree crickets, the broad-winged species is distinguished by its wider male wings compared to the narrow-winged tree cricket, and its preference for deciduous trees rather than the pine-loving pine tree cricket.
Among New England's tree crickets, the snowy tree cricket has the palest, most translucent appearance.
Among New England's tree crickets, the Four-spotted is the only one with exactly four dark spots on its body.
